steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on DRIVE, a protocol for automatically exploring a UGV's input space to collect training data for motion models. It should motivate why UGV motion modeling and data collection matter, describe the protocol and slip model, and state the contributions and experimental scope.

- Training data collection: manual driving, cost, standardization

steps.text:
- Motion modeling
  - modeling UGV motion fundamental for localization, path planning, path following
  - poor vehicle-terrain characterization -> significant modeling errors, possible system failure
  - limited information / sensory measurements on vehicle and ground properties -> reliable model hard
- Data collection
  - most models need training on empirical data to reduce modeling error
  - requires deploying UGV in operational environment, manual driving for extended period
  - energy consumption, deployment time critical -> facilitating this is important
  - standardizing could help comply with ISO 34502:2022(E) standard on autonomous navigation
  - most work relies on manual driving, little to no details on driving protocol
- DRIVE
  - protocol to facilitate and standardize vehicle characterization w.r.t. terrain (Figure 1)
  - identify true vehicle input space, differs from manufacturer's specifications
  - automatically send commands to cover entire true input space
  - vs. manual driving: covers mostly forward driving (red dots, our previous work)
  - broad input-space coverage -> significant modeling error reduction vs narrow coverage
  - train learned vehicle slip model: UGV commands -> body velocities
  - trained parameters vary significantly by terrain (green and blue diamond areas in Figure 1: gravel, snow)
- Contributions
  - (i) DRIVE: standardized UGV characterization and motion data generation protocol, training on entire input space
  - (ii) novel slip-based UGV motion prediction model: accuracy of model-based + minimal characterization requirement of learning-based
  - validation: three distinct UGV, weights 75\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} to 470\text{\,}\mathrm{kg}; two ground interactions (wheels, tracks); four terrain types
  - driving data totaling 7\text{\,}\mathrm{km} and 1.8\text{\,}\mathrm{h}

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Being able to model the motion of a UGV is fundamental for enabling localization, path planning and path following. If the vehicle-terrain characterization is poor, this will lead to significant modeling errors, and it can potentially cause system failure. Since there is limited information and limited sensory measurements available on vehicle and ground properties, it is still challenging to generate a reliable UGV motion model. Most models need to be trained on empirical data to reduce the modeling error. To do this you need to deploy the UGV in its operational environment and drive it manually for an extended period. Energy consumption and deployment time are critical for various UGV applications, so making this task easier is very important. Standardizing this process could also help engineers make sure their systems comply with the ISO 34502:2022(E) standard on autonomous navigation.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Being able to model the motion of a UGV is fundamental for enabling localization, path planning and path following. If the vehicle-terrain characterization is poor, this will lead to significant modeling errors, and it can potentially cause system failure. Since there is limited information and limited sensory measurements available on vehicle and ground properties, it is still challenging to generate a reliable UGV motion model. Most models need to be trained on empirical data to reduce the modeling error. To do this you need to deploy the UGV in its operational environment and drive it manually for an extended period. Energy consumption and deployment time are critical for various UGV applications, so making this task easier is very important. Standardizing this process could also help engineers make sure their systems comply with the ISO 34502:2022(E) standard on autonomous navigation.

Most work on UGV motion modeling uses manual driving to gather a training dataset, and gives little to no details on the driving protocol. So we propose DRIVE, a protocol that aims to facilitate and standardize vehicle characterization with respect to the terrain, as illustrated in Figure 1. First we identify the true input space of the vehicle, which is different from the manufacturer's specifications. Then we automatically send commands to the UGV so that the entire true input space is covered. This is different from the common approach of manual driving, which tends to cover only forward driving, as shown by the red dots that represent our previous work. We show that broad coverage of the input space gives a significant reduction in modeling error compared to narrow coverage. With this dataset, we train a learned vehicle slip model that maps UGV commands to the resulting body velocities. The trained parameters that result vary significantly depending on the terrain, as the green and blue diamond areas in Figure 1 show, which represent navigation on gravel and snow respectively.

The specific contributions of this paper are (i) DRIVE, a standardized UGV characterization and motion data generation protocol that allows motion models to be trained on the entire vehicle input space; (ii) A novel slip-based UGV motion prediction model, which leverages the accuracy of model-based approaches and the minimal system characterization requirement of learning-based approaches. We validate our contributions with an extensive experimental evaluation that has three distinct UGV, with weights ranging from 75\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} to 470\text{\,}\mathrm{kg}, two types of ground interaction (i.e., wheels and tracks) and four different terrain types. Our observations rely on driving data that totals 7\text{\,}\mathrm{km} and 1.8\text{\,}\mathrm{h}.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The ability to model the motion of UGV is fundamental to enabling localization [1], path planning [2] and path following [3]. Poor vehicle-terrain characterization will lead to significant modeling errors, potentially causing system failure [4]. With limited available information and sensory measurements on vehicle and ground properties, generating a reliable UGV motion model remains challenging. For most models, training on empirical data is required to reduce modeling error [5], which requires deploying a UGV in its operational environment and manually driving it for an extended period [6]. Since energy consumption and deployment time are critical for various UGV applications, facilitating this task is highly important. Standardizing this process could additionally help engineers ensure that their systems comply with the ISO 34502:2022(E) standard on autonomous navigation.

Most work on UGV motion modeling relies on manual driving to gather a training dataset, with little to no details on the driving protocol. Thus, we propose DRIVE, a protocol aiming to facilitate and standardize vehicle characterization with respect to the terrain, as illustrated in Figure 1. We start by identifying the vehicle's true input space, which differs from the manufacturer's specifications. We then automatically send commands to the UGV to cover the entire true input space. This differs from the common manual driving approach, which tends to cover only forward driving, as shown by the red dots representing our previous work [7]. We show that broad input-space coverage offers significant modeling error reduction compared to narrow coverage. With this dataset, we train a learned vehicle slip model that maps UGV commands to resulting body velocities. The resulting trained parameters vary significantly depending on terrain, as highlighted by the green and blue diamond areas in Figure 1, which represent navigation on gravel and snow respectively.

The specific contributions of this paper are (i) DRIVE, a standardized UGV characterization and motion data generation protocol allowing motion models to be trained on the entire vehicle input space; (ii) A novel slip-based UGV motion prediction model, leveraging the accuracy of model-based approaches and the minimal system characterization requirement of learning-based approaches. We validate our contributions with an extensive experimental evaluation featuring three distinct UGV, with weights ranging from 75\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} to 470\text{\,}\mathrm{kg}, two types of ground interaction (i.e., wheels and tracks) and four different terrain types. Our observations rely on driving data totaling 7\text{\,}\mathrm{km} and 1.8\text{\,}\mathrm{h}.
